title: Diagnosis of Asymptomatic Biliary Ascariasis by Abdominal Ultrasound in a Non-Endemic Area
case_text:
An 86-year-old man with a past medical history of prostate cancer in remission after radiotherapy, arterial hypertension, and chronic pulmonary obstructive disease presented to the primary care health system for his annual medical evaluation. The patient did not have any complaints, such as fever, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, jaundice, or pruritus. He did not notice any worms in his stools, nor any aggravated respiratory symptoms. Physical examination was normal.
He previously worked as a farmer and was living in a rural area of Portugal, where he consumed well water. He only traveled outside of Europe to India in 1955 for military duty, where he stayed for two years. He was never diagnosed or received any treatment for a parasitic infection.
The complete blood count showed isolated eosinophilia of 0,52 x103/muL; the hepatic function panel and liver enzymes were not altered.
A routine abdominal ultrasound was performed, which revealed normal liver parenchyma, without focal lesions, with discrete dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts. There was thickening of the gallbladder wall, with visualization of hyperechoic structures inside it with hypoechoic center lines like a rail, creating a tubular coiled appearance, without acoustic shadowing, and with apparent writhing movements (Figure 1). The main bile duct was normal. These imaging findings were compatible with biliary ascariasis. A chest radiograph was performed, and it did not show any significant alterations.
He was treated with 400 mg of oral albendazole in a single dose. Stool examination was only possible after treatment. No adult worms or eggs were visualized, on direct microscopy and following concentration techniques.
A complete resolution of the eosinophilia on the blood count was observed. A new abdominal ultrasound did not show any endoluminal content in the gallbladder.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Soil-Transmitted Helminths
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: asymptomatic biliary ascariasis
